processing: Grown in full sun, then steamed, rolled and dried in the usual sencha way; steaming replaced pan-firing in Yame during the Meiji period.
harvest_season: Spring, as with other Japanese sencha; the first flush is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Glossy, deep green needles, as is typical of well-made sencha.
appearance_wet: Soft, bright green leaf pieces, typical of sencha.
taste_profile: Yame teas are known for deep umami and natural sweetness with a clean finish; sencha adds a balance of gentle bitterness to that sweetness.

brewing.notes: Typical sencha approach: cool water brings out sweetness, hotter water brings out bitterness. Pour out every last drop between steeps.

vintage_note: Sold like other Japanese sencha, as the current year's harvest, with first-flush spring tea at the top of the range. It is meant to be drunk fresh, so check the picking year and keep an opened bag airtight and cool.
description:
Yame in southern Fukuoka is better known for gyokuro than for anything else, but sencha is the everyday face of the district. It is the same full-sun green tea made all over Japan, grown here in a warm climate where mountain slopes bring big swings between day and night, plenty of rain and frequent fog.

Unlike gyokuro and kabuse, sencha is not shaded before picking. The leaf is steamed, rolled and dried, and that gives a cup where bitterness and sweetness sit next to each other instead of the thick savouriness of a shaded tea.

Expect a rounded, umami-leaning green tea with a clean finish rather than anything sharp. The common mistake is water that is too hot, which pushes the bitterness forward; start around 70°C and raise the temperature in later steeps if you want more bite.

The name covers a whole district, so what you get varies a lot. Okuyame, the mountainous Kamiyo area, offers single-origin lots from different soils and cultivars, and those are the ones worth seeking out over a generic blend. Look for the harvest year and the area on the bag.
history:
Yame's own account starts in 1423, when the Zen monk Eirin Shuzui is said to have returned from Ming China with tea seeds and settled in what is now the Kurogi part of Yame, founding Reigan-ji temple with a village head's support and teaching tea-making there. The story is the district's founding tradition, and 2023 was marked as its 600th anniversary.

Tea reached ordinary households during the Edo period. In the Meiji period production moved from pan-fired to steamed green tea, the change that made sencha and gyokuro of the modern kind possible here, and gyokuro brought Yame its reputation at national competitions.
